title: Matured Sorghum Porridge
author: Laker Grace
desc: Half a kilo of sorghum flour stirred into two litres of boiling water until the colour turns black and a foam rises, then diluted, covered and left to stand twelve hours before drinking.
longDesc: Sorghum is a northern Ugandan staple, and this porridge is matured rather than just cooked: after the boil it is diluted, covered and left to sit for twelve hours, which changes it. The doneness cue for the cooking stage is precise and unusual — you stir until the colour changes to black and a foamy liquid rises to the top. Then it rests, and it is that resting that gives the drink its character.
ingredients: Cold water, for mixing and for diluting
steps: Bring the 2 litres of water to the boil.
Mix the sorghum flour into cold water until it is lump-free.
Add that to the hot water, stirring, until the colour changes to black and a foamy liquid rises to the top.
Pour it into a medium pot and dilute with cold water.
Cover it and let it sit for 12 hours before serving.
chefTips: The colour turning black and the foam rising are the two cues together. That is when the cooking stage is finished.
Twelve hours covered is the recipe, not a suggestion. It is what makes this matured sorghum porridge rather than sorghum porridge.
Mix the flour into cold water until genuinely lump-free before it goes anywhere near the heat.
Dilute after cooking and before the rest, not at the end.
It sits at room temperature, covered. That is what the source describes.
Sorghum grains are smaller than maize but have a similarly starchy endosperm, and the grain features in many staple dishes in northern Uganda.
Half a kilo of flour to two litres makes a substantial batch, which suits something that has to sit overnight anyway.
commonMistakes: Adding dry flour to the boiling water.
Stopping before the colour change and the foam.
Diluting it after the rest rather than before.
Leaving it uncovered while it sits.
sources: Adapted from 'Matured Sorghum Porridge', p8 of 'Traditional Products and Dishes: Uganda — From Earth to Table', second edition 2018, Slow Food International — the 2 litres of water, 500 g of sorghum flour, the cold-water lump-free mix, the colour-changes-to-black-and-foam-rises doneness cue, the dilution and the 12-hour covered rest are all as printed there.

The local names muwemba and mugusha, and the note that sorghum grains are smaller than maize but have a similar starchy endosperm and feature in many staple dishes in northern Uganda, are from the same entry.
storage: Refrigerate up to 2 days after its rest.
reheating: Drink it as it is, warm or cool. Do not re-boil.
healthBenefits: Sorghum is high in fibre, iron, magnesium and B vitamins, and is naturally gluten-free.
The long rest begins a light fermentation, which makes the minerals more available.
No fat, no dairy and no added sugar.
A drought-tolerant grain, which is why it anchors diets in the drier north.
culturalNote: Sorghum does the work in northern and north-eastern Uganda that banana does in the centre — it grows where little else will, and it turns up as stiff porridge, as this drink, and as the base of the region's beers. The twelve-hour rest is the same instinct that produces obushera and enturire: time doing work that heat cannot.
